title: NGC 5256
caption: The merging galaxies NGC 5256, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 5256 · constellation Ursa Major · about 350 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration and A. Evans (University of Virginia, Charlottesville/NRAO/Stony Brook University)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Streamers of gas surround the two nuclei in this Hubble image, and blue spiral trails mark places where stars have recently formed. This is NGC 5256, also called Markarian 266, a pair of disc galaxies on the verge of merging, about 350 million light-years away in Ursa Major, the Great Bear.

The whole system is badly disturbed, and observations in infrared, millimetre-wave and radio light add evidence of a starburst, a burst of star formation. Each galaxy also holds an active galactic nucleus, a sign that the turmoil is letting gas fall toward their central black holes while also feeding new stars.
X-rays add another layer. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory found that both nuclei, and a region of hot gas between them, have been heated by shock waves as gas clouds slam together at high speed.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.56 x 2.56 arcminutes) and distance (350 million light years), the frame spans roughly 261,000 × 261,000 light-years. Its light set out about 350 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using a blue filter and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the shock-heated gas shows up only in X-rays.

alt: Two galaxy centres surrounded by streamers of gas and blue spiral trails of new stars.
